rationale: Queens is a tiny, hot, recursion-heavy benchmark (7 functions, ~768 text bytes) whose core work sits in the backtracking loop of Try, so control-flow-centric passes dominate the table: FLA and BCF get the highest SecurityGain/DiversityGain weights because flattening and bogus-edge insertion most disrupt the recovery of the nested recursive search structure, and the absolute size and runtime budget of a 768-byte binary tolerates their typical 2-5x inflation cheaply, hence only moderate RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights. SUB is nearly free and correct, so it gets a permissive low-cost profile to run broadly across all small functions. IGV cheaply hides the board-state globals from static analysis, so it stays enabled with low cost weights. IBR and ICALL are kept at mid-tier weights: they add real per-branch/per-call runtime overhead on the hot recursive path, and this program has few call sites, limiting ICALL's payoff, so they should fire selectively on feature-favoring functions only. SPLIT is deliberately low across the board because its benefit shrinks on functions as small as these (Try is only 258 bytes), so it is effectively demoted to a diversity garnish. All CorrectnessRisk weights are held low to reflect that these passes are mature, but FLA carries the highest risk weight since flattening the invariant-laden Try loop is the one place miscompilation would actually bite.
